questions.problem:
The mass $M(t),$ in micrograms, of a sample of manganese-53 is given by

$$
M(t)=17{e}^{-0.187t},
$$

where $t$ is the time, in millions of years. Rounded to one decimal place, what is the half-life of manganese-53?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

We're given that $k=0.187.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1/2} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{0.187} \\  & ≈3.7\,\text{million years}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The half-life of polonium-210 is $138.4$ days. How long does it take for a $8.8\,\mu \text{g}$ sample of polonium-210 to reduce to $1.1\,\mu \text{g}?$ Do not round the answer.

$t=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{days}$
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=138.4$ days, we have

$$
138.4=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{138.4}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=8.8\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=8.8{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/138.4}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=1.1\,\mu \text{g}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1.1 & =8.8{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/138.4}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1.1 & =8.8{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/138.4} \\ \frac{1.1}{8.8} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/138.4} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/138.4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/138.4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{138.4} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{138.4} \\ t & =\frac{138.4\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =\frac{138.4\cdot 3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =415.2\,\text{days}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=1.1\,\mu \text{g}.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{1.1\,\mu \text{g}}{8.8\,\mu \text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $3$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $8.8\,\mu \text{g}$ to $1.1\,\mu \text{g}.$ Hence,

$$
t=3\cdot {t}_{1/2}=3\cdot 138.4=415.2\,\text{days}.
$$

{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=50\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
50=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=400\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=50\,\mu \text{g}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
50=400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}\,\,
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}50 & =400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \frac{50}{400} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50} \\ t & =\frac{50\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =150.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
t=3\cdot {t}_{1/2}=3\cdot 50\,\text{s}=150\,\text{s}.

\begin{aligned}0.25{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/2.6} \\ 0.25\cancel{{M}_{0}} & =\cancel{{M}_{0}}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/2.6} \\ 0.25 & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/2.6} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.25) & =ln\,({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/2.6}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.25) & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2.6} \\ t & =-\frac{2.6\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.25)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈5.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the tracer is approximately $5.2$ years old.

canonical_examples.problem: The half-life of bismuth-210 is $5.012$ days. How long does it take for a $1\,280\,\textrm g$ sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to $5\,\textrm g?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that $t_{1/2} = 5.012$ days we have

$$
5.012 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{5.012}
$$

Also, since $M_0 = 1\,280\,\textrm g,$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t) = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
5 = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =1\,280{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{5}{1\,280} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{1}{256} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{256}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ t & =\frac{5.012\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡256}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{5\,\text{g}}{1\,280\,\text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{256} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{8},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t) =  \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $8$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $1\,280\,\textrm g$ to $5\,\textrm g.$ Hence,

$$
t = 8\cdot t_{1/2} =8 \cdot 5.012 \approx 40.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$
